name: Minimal number of vertices in a triangle-free graph with chromatic number n.
comment: Mycielski's construction proves that this sequence is infinite.
Harary states in an exercise (12.19) that a(4) <= 11. Chvátal proves that a(4) = 11 and gives a proof of uniqueness. Jensen & Royle prove that a(5) = 22.
Goedgebeur proves that 32 <= a(6) <= 40. - _Charles R Greathouse IV_, Mar 06 2018
reference: F. Harary, Graph Theory, Addison-Wesley, Reading, Mass. (1969), p. 149.
link: V. Chvátal, The minimality of the Mycielski graph, Graphs and combinatorics (Proc. Capital Conf., George Washington Univ., Washington, D.C., 1973), Ed. by R. A. Bari and F. Harary, pp. 243-246. Lecture Notes in Mathematics 406, Springer, Berlin, 1974.
Ewan Davies and Freddie Illingworth, The chi-Ramsey problem for triangle-free graphs, arXiv preprint (2021). arXiv:2107.12288 [math.CO]

Geoffrey Exoo and Jan Goedgebeur, Bounds for the smallest k-chromatic graphs of given girth, Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science DMTCS vol. 21:3, 2019, #9. arXiv:1805.06713 [math.CO]
T. Jensen and G. F. Royle, Small graphs with chromatic number 5, A computer search, Journal of Graph Theory 19 (1995), pp. 107-116.
J. Mycielski, Sur le coloriage des graphes, Colloq. Math. 3 (1955), pp. 161-162.
Gordon Royle, Smallest triangle-free graph with chromatic number 5 (2018)
formula: For n > 3, the Mycielskian of a graph for a(n-1) shows that a(n) <= 2*a(n-1) + 1. This can be used to show that a(n) <= 3/4 * 2^n - 1 for n > 1.
a(n) >> n^2 log n. In particular, Davies & Illingworth (Theorem 1) can be used to show that a(n) > k*n^2 log n for any k < 1/2 and large enough n. - _Charles R Greathouse IV_, Jan 05 2026
Exoo & Goedgebeur prove that a(n) >= 2n - 2 (p. 2, set g = 4 under even girth) and a(n) >= a(n-1) + 3n/2 - 2 (Lemma 1). - _Charles R Greathouse IV_, Jan 05 2026
example: The unique graph for a(1) = 1 is a lone vertex.
The unique graph for a(2) = 2 is two vertices connected by an edge.
The unique graph for a(3) = 5 is the cycle graph C_5 (the pentagon).
The unique graph for a(4) = 11 is the Grötzsch graph.
There are 80 graphs for a(5) = 22, see the Jensen & Royle link, the Royle link, and the Chen link.
